1. Charlie Meadows is hosting a radio show called Brunch with Charlie Listen to the first part of the program and write the information in the spaces below.

Hi there. How are you doing?
It is Charlie Meadows here again and with me on Brunchwood Charlie this morning are two guests, both from the special committee that has just been set up to find a twin city for Hong Kong.
I’m very pleased to have with me Dr Emily Lee He, who is a member of Legislative Council of Hong Kong.
Welcome Dr Lee.
Good morning, Charlie.
Glad to be here.
And also with me is Lemme Chan.
Hi. Now, Lemme is an undergraduate student at Hong Kong University.
And what is it that you’re studying, Lemme?
Uh, History. Oh yes, history.
I had it noted down somewhere.
somewhere. Now let’s start with you, Dr Lee.
You have been appointed the chairperson of this special committee which has just been set up.
Would you like to tell us about that?
Certainly. Well, as you say it’s a committee set up especially to choose a twin city for Hong Kong.
OK, now a lot of our listeners won’t have heard of the idea of twin cities so maybe Maybe you could explain what it is.
OK, yes, well the other name for a twin city you might have heard of is the sister city.
OK, yes, I’ve heard sister city before yeah.
OK, so when two cities decide they want to be twin cities they enter into an agreement.
And the important thing is that to be twin cities the two cities have to be in different countries.
All right, so not two cities in the same country Yeah that’s right and there are thousands of towns and cities twint with each other across the world OK, so when did this all start then, twin cities?
And why did cities want to twin?
Well, that’s a good question, maybe let me should give a bit of the historical background.
Oh, OK. Well, the idea of twin cities, at least our concept of it in the modern era, started just after World War II.
OK, but why then?
Why were twin Cities so important after the war?
Didn’t people have better things to be doing rebuilding houses and everything?
Well, twin cities were seen as part of a wider initiative at that time to promote peace and understanding.
So it had a serious point to it So does that mean that twin cities were in countries which were fighting each other during the war?
That's right, in countries which were until a couple of years before that fighting each other.
Wow. That can’t have been easy.
So did it work?
Was it successful?
Well, a lot of cities certainly took part.
Obviously during the war many countries had suffered.
On the one side you had Japan, Germany, Italy and on the other you had, like, the United States, the UK, France and the Soviet Union.
And the most common twinning of cities was actually between France and Germany, many, two countries that had been the fiercest of enemies through history.
Why was that?
I’m sure there must be a good reason.
Well I think just on a practical level, these countries are next to each other and so it was easy for them to communicate with each other.
Well that makes sense.
So thinking about nowadays, a city typically pairs up with just one city?
Is that what happens?
Well it all depends.
Usually a small town, you know, of a few thousand people would usually twin with just one other town.
But there are some towns in Europe that are incredibly popular as a twin town.
There’s this one town called twinned with more than one city, but certainly not thirty.
Say four or five.
Ten would be unusual.
Right, so Hong Kong is now looking for its first twin city, so what do you hope to achieve?
Maybe I could answer this.
The first thing we want to achieve is to encourage an exchange of culture.
An exchange of culture sounds nice.
But what does it mean exactly?
Exactly. Well, the obvious ones are language and food.
I mean Hong Kong has a variety of languages and lots of amazing food that we can share with the future twin city.
Nice! What else?
Well, another aim is related to commerce.
It’s the promotion of business links.
So what kind of business links?
It can be any kind really.
For instance, Hong Kong is really good at banking, I mean obviously, and another area which I find quite exciting is fashion design.
Really? Wow, that’s quite glamorous then.
Yeah, it would be great to be twinned with one of the fashion design capitals of the world.
Yeah, and maybe I could come with you!
Right, we’re going to take a short music break and we'll be back in a couple of minutes.
That is the end of Task 1.
1. You now have one minute to tidy up your answers.

Now, Dr Lee you wanted to make a special announcement.
Is that right?
Yes, that’s right.
As you said the committee has just been set up and we are looking for more people, more members of the general public to join the committee.
So I’m here to ask your listeners if they would be interested in getting involved in choosing a twin city for Hong Kong by coming on to the committee.
Can it be anyone?
Well there are going to be three groups of people on the committee: politicians, students, and a general public.
What were the exact numbers we are looking for, Lamy?
Um, Yes, we're looking for five students and five members of the general public.
Yeah, that’s right.
And we would be delighted if the listeners of your radio show applied.
Great. So what about students?
Is it open to primary school students?
No that’s a bit young, it’s open to secondary school students and university students.
So secondary school and university students, right?
That's right. So what about the members of the general public?
Any age limits?
Well for the general public group if you want to reply, you have to be retired.
Retired! Now that’s what I call an age limit!
it. Why so?
Well one reason is that they have more time than people who are working.
Ah, you mean more time to attend the meetings?
No, not really.
What I mean is time to do some research.
That sort of thing.
But more importantly, they have a lot of life experience to offer.
Oh, OK. So you senior citizens, if you're listening we want you.
OK, and what kind Well, we are looking for two qualities in all the applicants.
OK. We are looking for someone with knowledge of Hong Kong.
Ah I see, so they can share this knowledge of Hong Kong with the twin city, right?
Yes, and the second quality is they should have a real enthusiasm for other cultures.
Yeah, I can see that, yes.
I mean, we'd really want to have people on board who have that, you know, enthusiasm for cultures for other countries.
Great. Oh, I have another question.
Do people applying for the committee have to be from Hong Kong?
Actually no, They can be any nationality.
As long as they have been living in Hong Kong for at least three years.
That's fine. I see, so open to any nationality but must have been here for 3 years, Well it all sounds awesome to me.
So how do listeners apply for a place on the committee and what's the deadline?
Let me. do you have the details there?
Yeah, um, applications are open now and they should be submitted online.
The deadline is the 30th of June.
So online applications.
By the end of June.
Yes, that’s right.
Gotcha. Wait a minute.
You said politicians before.
What about the politicians on the committee?
Are you choosing them too?
Well, the politicians on the committee have already been chosen.
Already been chosen?
Why is that?
Well, we want to represent all the political parties in Hong Kong.
OK, I suppose that’s fair to try to represent all the political parties.
Absolutely. OK, so many thanks to you both.
And maybe we can have you back in the studio sometime in the future to tell our listeners which city was chosen.
chosen. Yes, that would be great.
That is the end of Task 2.

Video 1: Maria from Buenos Aires, Argentina
Hello Hong Kong!
I'm Maria from Buenos Aires in Argentina.
Choose Buenos Aires and come sample our culture.
Here I am in a tango class.
When people think of Argentina the first thing they think of is tango dancing.
dancing. The tango has a very rich history.
Although it's considered a high -class dance now, it started in lower -class districts in the 19th Century.
Most of the people who danced it were men, which meant men often danced with other men.
Why did they do this?
Well, for many men their wives or girlfriends were in Europe and they came alone to Argentina.
So they had to choose between not dancing at all or dancing with men.
The second major area of culture in Argentina is, of course, football and here I am at a Boca Juniors football stadium in one of their hospitality boxes.
Now, there are three great reasons for you to spend the day at a Boca Juniors hospitality box on a match day.
Most important is you can see the game.
Of course, you can see football all over the world but what's extraordinary here is to witness the passion of a football match here in Argentina.
The passion it’s like no other place in the world.
At the same time you can enjoy our most famous food
our Our beef sandwiches have won prizes for being the best sandwiches in the world.
And finally, as part of your experience, you will personally meet and spend the game with a famous ex -player of Boca Juniors.
Of course, it’s not unusual for ex -players to meet guests at matches nowadays.
But here at Boca, the ex -player will spend time with you and explain as you watch the game.
game. So you will be able to learn from a legendary ex -player as he explains the game to you as it happens.
Thanks for listening Hong Kong and choose when is Aries?
Video 2: Piotra from Crackoff, Poland
Hello Hong Kong.
This is Piotra here, or rather Peter.
I’m from Crackoff in Poland and I’m going to show you why you should choose Krakoff to be Hong Kong’s twin city.
First of all Krakoff is great for tourism and we can share a lot of information with you about how to promote tourism.
Let me show you some examples.
Krakoff was the capital of Poland about 650 years ago when Poland had kings.
Where did the old Kings live?
Have a look Of course, the royal castle that you see now has changed many times in 650 years, What you see today is very different to what the castle looked
like before. For example, 300 years ago there was a huge fire and half the castle was destroyed.
Can you imagine?
Half of the Royal Castle!
Destroyed! And 150 years ago the walls were taken down.
Why? Why? Well because the city was expanding and so building material was needed for all the new buildings.
And so the walls, which had stood for hundreds of years, were taken down.
Now I'm in the main square in Krakow.
In the centre of the square that building you can see is the old Central Market.
Until about a hundred years ago, it used to sell mainly clothes, I mean lots of things of course, but mainly clothes.
But what about now?
Well, as crack -off attracts millions of tourists a year the market sells arts and crafts for tourists.
It does sell other things but arts and crafts are the main attraction.
And there are lots and lots of restaurants where you can get something to eat and also bars and cafes to get a drink.
The really striking thing is that many of these are underground and under the square!
What a good use of the space!
The second thing we can offer you is culture.
Here I am in a district of Krakow called Novahuta, which in English means New Factory.
As you can see there are lots of factories here and they mainly produce steel.
But what about culture?
Well, this city was built in 1949 by the communist government and because it was built during that time it has communist architecture.
Tourists and particularly architecture students from all over the world actually visit here to see the architecture.
Isn’t it amazing that ugly buildings are now tourist attractions!
I hope that you have enjoyed this video and that you will choose crack off.
Goodbye!
That is the end of Task 3.

it’s time for our special guest today.
Today I’m very happy to have back Ms Lemme Chan from Hong Kong University.
Thank you. Now, I've never been to Poland or Krakow and I’m sure a lot of our listeners haven’t either.
So maybe to start with, what were your first impressions of Krakow?
Well, from the moment I first arrived, the people in Krakow were really generous.
Right. I mean, I lived with a host family, you know, and they were so generous and so were their friends In what way?
Well, I mean, everyone invited me into their homes, and you know, made me feel just very welcome.
It was very different to Hong Kong.
I mean, here you don’t normally get invited to someone’s home.
You were saying before before we came on air that it can be pretty cold in Poland.
So was the weather cold all the time?
Sometimes the temperature got down to minus 32 degrees!
Wow, how did you cope!
Well actually it wasn’t that bad.
When you’re inside, the heating’s turned on all the time.
And Sometimes it’s actually too warm and you have to open a window.
What? Even when it’s minus 32 outside?
Yeah, exactly! And when you are outside you wear thermal underwear, you know, like that special winter underwear, so you're always warm.
So if you do visit Poland in winter take your thermal underwear that’s my advice.
Well, you've heard it here first listeners!
So you said your host family were nice.
What about people in general?
Actually, most people were very friendly.
Only most You make it sound like some people weren't.
No, not at all, not at all, though there was one particular incident.
Oh yes, and what happened then?
Well, I was in a cafe and I was ordering something to drink.
And I said to the waiter in Polish, I said dvah habata prussia which means in Polish two teas please And the waiter said de vie.
Apparently, I had made a grammatical mistake when I said the word for two and he the waiter, I mean seemed actually quite angry about it.
It was like if you are going to speak our language then you must speak it properly!
I was so shocked and embarrassed.
There was me trying my best to speak Polish and he was so intolerant.
Apparently, everything had to be grammatically perfect.
At least I was trying to speak the language!
Hmm. and you were telling me earlier about a big adventure you had on your skiing trip.
Oh, yes. And actually, this is a better example of how nice the people in Poland are.
Me and the daughter of the host family, Julia, we decided to go skiing.
Actually we tried to go the Sunday before but we got this really really slow train on the Sunday morning that stopped everywhere.
I think it stopped at 52 different stations!
So by the time we got there it was too late to ski.
So the next Sunday we decided to get the bus instead.
And was that better than the train?
Yeah, much better.
We got there by 9 in the morning.
morning. So had you ever skied before then?
No, I hadn't.
No, neither have I.
How did you find it?
Well, if you've never been skiing, there are easy slopes for beginners and children.
So I was on the easy slopes in the morning and that was OK, but then after lunch I got on the wrong lift and ended up at the top of a really difficult slope.
Oh no! And there was no way down except to ski down!
Oh no! And did you fall?
Yeah! Again and again.
I thought I was going to die.
I was terrified!
Well, you’re braver than I would have been.
I don’t know about that.
I got to the bottom and I didn’t ski again.
I just sat in the cafe and drank hot chocolate all afternoon.
So that was your ski adventure.
Well, actually, that wasn’t all.
So what else happened?
Well, we were on the bus coming back and it was late evening.
We were about an hour from Krakow, the weather was really bad.
I mean, lots of snow, and the bus broke down.
Oh dear! It wouldn’t have been that bad but I was actually going to give a talk about Hong Kong to a school in Krakow at 9 o 'clock in the morning the day after on the Monday morning, and
I really didn’t want to miss the talk and let everyone down.
Oh no. So what happened next?
Well, as luck would have it, the host family had a cousin who lived nearby, and Julia called him and he said he would help us.
And did he?
Did you get back on time for your talk?
Actually I did.

And you're not going to believe this, and I’m not sure I believe it myself, but the cousin was a farmer and after Julia called him, we waited and waited waited and waited and finally he turned up in his
tractor! His tractor!
Yeah and he drove us all the way back to Krakow in his tractor.
It turns out the tractors are really great for travelling in heavy snow.
It took us about three hours but we got back to Krakow and I managed to make it in time for my talk.
I mean, it was really nice of him.
The cousin, Well that’s a great story.
OK, so thanks again Lemmy, for dropping in.

amazing. It’s taken us only 4 years to finish it.

and um litter.

Norman? Ah, thanks Anne for bringing this up.

touched. So I said 50%.

the experts we consulted said no vehicles and roads either.
